content: Endometrial adenocarcinoma, commonly referred to as womb cancer, is a malignant tumor that arises from the lining of the uterus, known as the endometrium. It is distinct from uterine sarcomas, which are tumors originating from the muscle layer of the uterus. The prognosis for patients with endometrial cancer largely depends on the risk of microscopic metastases that may remain after surgical treatment. Adjuvant chemotherapy, which is administered after surgery, has been shown to improve survival in certain types of adenocarcinomas, and there is evidence suggesting that endometrial cancer is responsive to cytotoxic chemotherapy. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the impact of adjuvant chemotherapy on survival outcomes in patients with endometrial cancer who have undergone a hysterectomy. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to August 2010. Additional sources, such as clinical trial registries, conference abstracts, reference lists of relevant studies, and consultations with experts, were also utilized. The review focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared adjuvant chemotherapy with either other adjuvant treatments or no additional treatment. The data from the included studies were analyzed using a random-effects meta-analysis. Hazard ratios (HRs) were calculated to assess overall survival and progression-free survival, while risk ratios (RRs) were used to compare death rates and the sites of initial cancer recurrence. Five RCTs compared the outcomes of patients who received no additional treatment after hysterectomy and radiotherapy with those who received additional chemotherapy. Four other trials directly compared platinum-based combination chemotherapy with radiotherapy. When survival data from 2,197 women were pooled, the results demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in overall survival with the use of adjuvant chemotherapy. Specifically, the relative risk (RR) of death was 0.88 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.79 to 0.99), indicating a survival benefit. A sensitivity analysis focusing on trials that used modern platinum-based chemotherapy regimens showed an even greater benefit, with a relative risk of death of 0.85 (95% CI: 0.76 to 0.96). This corresponds to an absolute risk reduction of 4% (ranging from 1% to 8%) and a number needed to treat (NNT) of 25 to achieve one additional beneficial outcome. The hazard ratio (HR) for overall survival was 0.74 (95% CI: 0.64 to 0.89), favoring the addition of postoperative platinum-based chemotherapy. Similarly, the HR for progression-free survival was 0.75 (95% CI: 0.64 to 0.89), indicating that chemotherapy reduces the risk of death or disease progression by approximately 25%. Furthermore, chemotherapy was found to decrease the risk of developing the first recurrence outside the pelvis, with a relative risk of 0.79 (95% CI: 0.68 to 0.92), corresponding to a 5% absolute risk reduction and an NNT of 20. While the analysis of pelvic recurrence rates was underpowered, the data suggested that chemotherapy might be less effective than radiotherapy in preventing pelvic recurrences when directly compared (RR: 1.28, 95% CI: 0.97 to 1.68). However, when chemotherapy was used in combination with radiotherapy, there appeared to be an added benefit, with a relative risk of 0.48 (95% CI: 0.20 to 1.18), although this finding was not statistically significant. In conclusion, postoperative platinum-based chemotherapy provides a modest but significant improvement in both progression-free survival and overall survival for patients with endometrial cancer, regardless of whether radiotherapy is also administered. It reduces the risk of distant metastases and may serve as an alternative to radiotherapy in some cases. Additionally, it appears to have added value when used in conjunction with radiotherapy.
